decisions.check_result: Source confirms the path. resolve_camera (backend/cameras.py:159-160) and default_camera (cameras.py:131-132) admit only the caller's own private, active camera. _process_frame passes only the event dict to dispatch_live_alert (backend/app.py:533-534), and /analyze does the same through dispatch_alerts (app.py:582, 609). get_dispatcher (app.py:312-327) builds one actuator, one Notifier with the single telegram_chat_id, and one zone name. dispatch_live_alert and dispatch_alerts send the siren command (app.py:348, 375) and the evidence photo (app.py:356, 381; notifier.py:56-61) with no community, owner or admin_can_view check and no audit. Meanwhile the web paths enforce admin_can_view (app.py:282, 664) and audit admin views (app.py:726-731), and the owner is told the admin cannot see the camera (backend/pages.py:166-168). notification_channels and alert_deliveries (bd_intivision/schema_vigia.sql:227-262) are unused, and manage.py:57 supports any number of communities. I weighed design intent. The prototype notifier sends to a single phone ('avisa al celular'), the zone is 'Cuadra 01 - Piloto', and the operator who sets TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID is trusted with full DB access. So a one-community pilot whose chat holds only the operator crosses no boundary, and source cannot exclude that configuration. Nor does source establish it: the multi-tenant schema, the admin_can_view promise and create-community show the product supports several tenants. The decisive facts are chat membership and community/hidden-camera counts, both deployment state, so needs_validation is kept. I dropped the 'no code execution' blocker and the local plan: source already shows the dispatch behaviour plainly, and a mock harness would not resolve the decisive facts. I corrected the trace line for the Notifier (app.py:322) and added evidence for /analyze (609), settings.py:17 and manage.py:57.

Every cited line re-read and correct. config.yaml:45-52 selects mqtt on broker.hivemq.com:1883, topic guardian/demo7k3x9/siren, null credentials. settings.py:15-20 overrides only username/password. docker-compose.yml:19 and 37 mount config.yaml read-only. actuator.py:40-44 connects without TLS, with credentials only if set. The sketch connects anonymously over plaintext (sketch.ino:29, 86) and acts on any message (41-71): an 'ON' prefix with an unbounded toInt duration (52-58; ON:2592000 is about 30 days, and 32-bit wrap applies after about 19.7 days of uptime), WARN calls noTone (61), OFF calls allOff (65-66). I found a material limiting fact the hunter did not cite. As committed, the sketch joins the Wokwi-GUEST simulator WiFi (sketch.ino:20-21), and its header and the backend comments (sketch.ino:2; backend/app.py:333, 351) say the MQTT commands exist to be seen in the Wokwi simulation. So the repository shows only a simulated consumer, and 'physical siren' is not established; I reworded the title and description. Repository content alone cannot confirm the claim, because its impact depends on whether a physical device subscribes to the topic and on the public broker's anonymous access policy. Both are outside source, and probing them is prohibited. It is not rejected: the tracked config sends the production backend's alert commands to a public topic, and a field device on that topic is the product's stated purpose. I removed two non-decisive blockers (GitHub repository visibility, since a public broker's '#' wildcard exposes topics anyway; and inability to execute code) and the local plan, whose result source already shows. The deployment plan is now three owner-observed facts that must all hold.
